name: Polyacrylamide gel
lead: Polyacrylamide gel, in its injectable medical form polyacrylamide hydrogel (PAAG), is a water-based synthetic gel made of cross-linked polyacrylamide. It has been used as a permanent soft-tissue filler, including for facial contouring and for HIV-related facial fat loss, and the same type of material is used in other medical settings such as injections for urinary incontinence and, in a Danish trial, intra-articular injection for knee osteoarthritis [1][5][6][7][8].

Polyacrylamide itself is described as low in toxicity, but its precursor, the acrylamide monomer, is a recognised neurotoxin and carcinogen, and safety concerns about PAAG products have centred on possible residual monomer [2]. The FDA lists non-absorbable fillers as approved only for the nasolabial folds and cheek acne scars, and says removal of permanent fillers can be difficult or impossible [4].

One registered study follows 240 women who had polyacrylamide hydrogel removed from the breast and were reconstructed, which indicates that the material has been used for breast augmentation and has needed removal in some patients [9]. The sources contain no looksmaxxing forum discussion of PAAG as a facial filler.

paras: Polyacrylamide is a synthetic polymer of acrylamide units. Wikipedia describes it as a material of low toxicity that has been used as a subdermal filler for aesthetic facial surgery, noting concern about acrylamide contamination [2]. Hydrogels in general are cross-linked polymer networks that absorb large amounts of fluid and resemble living tissue, which is why they are used across biomedicine [10].

In aesthetics, the gel has been used as a permanent facial filler. A registered phase 3 study injected polyacrylamide hydrogel in HIV-related facial lipoatrophy (100 participants, begun 2005) [7]. The same material has been studied for urinary incontinence, with a randomised trial comparing it with tension-free vaginal tape, and in anal incontinence and vocal-fold laryngoplasty [5][6][11][12]. A 2024 randomised non-inferiority trial in Denmark compared an intra-articular polyacrylamide hydrogel with hyaluronic acid in knee osteoarthritis [8].

The FDA's dermal filler guidance lists nodules, granulomas, infection, migration and vascular injury among filler complications and states that some appear weeks to years after injection and that removal of permanent fillers can be difficult or impossible [4]. A systematic review of delayed complications after tear trough filler included polyacrylamide among its search terms, with most reported cases involving hyaluronic acid, poly-L-lactic acid or calcium hydroxylapatite [13].
A registered Chinese follow-up study of breast reconstruction after removal of injected polyacrylamide hydrogel enrolled 240 participants [9].

Facial-filler evidence in the sources is limited to the registration of a 100-participant study in HIV facial lipoatrophy, with no results given here [7]. Outside aesthetics, human trials include a randomised comparison with hyaluronic acid in knee osteoarthritis [8], a three-year follow-up of a randomised trial against vaginal tape for stress urinary incontinence [5], and a study of voice outcomes after laryngoplasty [11]. These concern other uses and do not establish outcomes for cosmetic filling.

card.summary: A permanent synthetic gel filler with little published cosmetic evidence in these sources; removal can be difficult.
card.note: Permanent fillers can be hard to remove; concerns centre on residual acrylamide monomer.

quick.overview:
Polyacrylamide gel is a water-rich synthetic gel that has been injected as a permanent filler for facial contouring and fat loss, and is also used in medicine for incontinence and, experimentally, knee osteoarthritis.

The sources contain few studies of its cosmetic use and no forum discussion. Evidence in other uses does not establish how it performs as a face filler.
quick.mechanism: The gel stays in place and adds volume as a non-absorbable bulking material.
quick.risks: Polyacrylamide is described as low in toxicity, but the acrylamide monomer is a neurotoxin and carcinogen, and contamination is a stated concern. The FDA says permanent fillers can cause nodules, migration and late complications and can be difficult or impossible to remove.
